title: Until certainty comes
hookLine: worship your Lord until certainty comes to you (15:99)

cards: Here's a pattern people describe. Someone starts a practice: praying, reading, sitting each morning. For a while it glows.
Then it doesn't. They're going through the motions, and a voice says: if you're not sure anymore, why keep doing it? Wait until you feel it again.
Surah al-Hijr ends with a verse that sounds, at first, like it agrees: worship your Lord until certainty comes to you. Some people have read it exactly that way.
Commentators like Ibn Kathir say that reading gets it backwards.

teach.b: First, where the verse comes from. Verse ninety-seven, in paraphrase: We know your chest is tight because of what they say.
The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ is being mocked in Mecca, and God's answer, in verses ninety-eight and ninety-nine, isn't argument. It's practice.
Glorify your Lord with praise, be among those who bow down. Then, in Pickthall's translation: "And serve thy Lord till the Inevitable cometh unto thee." Pickthall says the Inevitable.
The Arabic word is al-yaqin, certainty, the certain thing. Commentators such as Ibn Kathir say the certain thing here is death, the one event no one doubts.
They point to a scene in Bukhari: when a companion, 'Uthman ibn Maz'un, died, the Prophet said of him, as for him, al-yaqin has come to him.

teach.h: NOT WAIT, THEN STOP: KEEP GOING.
teach.b: So the verse doesn't say worship until you feel sure, then stop. It says keep worshiping for as long as you live.
Ibn Kathir, for one, rejects the reading that a person who reaches certainty can drop the prayer; the Prophet himself prayed until the end of his life. Yaqin, as a word, still matters a great deal.

The Qur'an speaks of knowledge of certainty, the eye of certainty, the truth of certainty, and later Sufi writers built a ladder of faith from those phrases. But this verse puts the practice first, not the feeling.
You don't wait for the glow to come back before you show up.
You show up, and keep showing up, until the one certain thing arrives. The verse measures a practice in a lifetime, not a mood.

how: Muslim scholars teach 15:99 as a call to keep up worship for the whole of life, reading al-yaqin as death, and they cite it against the idea that a person who reaches certainty may abandon the prayer.

o: certainty, the certain thing; here, read as death
a vision of the unseen granted only to prophets
a sure feeling of faith that ends the need to pray

games.q: until certainty comes — tap the pairs.

s: 15:99 means you can stop worshiping once you're sure
commentators such as Ibn Kathir read al-yaqin as death: keep worshiping as long as you live.
Pickthall translates al-yaqin here as 'the Inevitable'
serve thy Lord till the Inevitable cometh unto thee.

of 'Uthman ibn Maz'un: as for him, al-yaqin has come to him.

games.q: you're being mocked, and your chest is tight. what does God tell the Prophet to do, at the end of al-Hijr?
o: glorify your Lord, bow down, and keep worshiping.
games.why: glorify with praise, be among those who bow down, and serve your Lord until the certain thing comes.

practice: Maybe today you feel close, maybe you feel nothing at all; either way, sit, and don't check how it feels. Just keep the practice, the way you'd brush your teeth on a day you didn't feel like it.
If you pray, say subhanallah with each breath, and when your mind wanders, come back.

wordCard.voice: Yaqin. Certainty, the certain thing. In 15:99, commentators read it as death: keep worshiping until it comes. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: certainty, the certain thing; in 15:99 commentators read it as death.

carryVoice: Your line: until the certain thing comes. The glow can come and go. Four hundred fifty days, and counting.
